TabICL 2.2 imputation on Adult and Bank Marketing

Source: vignettes/tabiclImpute-benchmark.Rmd
tabiclImpute-benchmark.Rmd

Introduction

This benchmark is adapted from transformerImpute-benchmark.Rmd on the transformerImpute-rebased branch. It retains the Adult/Bank samples, common MCAR/MAR masks and scoring protocol, and compares kNN, ranger, ranger_seq10, xgboost, xgboost_seq10 and four TabICL variants: pretrained/fine-tuned, each with one or up to ten passes.

Like vimpute-benchmark.Rmd, this document is precomputed from its .Rmd.orig source using vignettes/precompute.R. The generated .Rmd contains static code examples, tables and figures. Package builds and checks render these cached outputs without loading Python or fitting models. Edit the .Rmd.orig source to change the experiment, then precompute again.

Models and regeneration

All four TabICL variants call vimpute(method = "tabicl2"), with PMM and residual noise disabled. Numeric targets use TabICLRegressor and factors use TabICLClassifier. Fine-tuning uses the corresponding Finetuned estimators. Each target and iteration fits a fresh model on observed target values only.

Method Fine-tuning Sequential passes
vimpute_tabicl2 No 1
vimpute_tabicl2_finetune Yes 1
vimpute_tabicl2_seq10 No Up to 10
vimpute_tabicl2_finetune_seq10 Yes Up to 10

All variants use eight inference ensemble members on CPU. Fine-tuning uses five epochs, learning rate 1e-5, patience three, and two ensemble members for training and validation, with mixed precision disabled. The upstream internal validation split never receives hidden imputation truth. The seq10 variants use sequential = TRUE, nseq = 10; vimpute’s convergence rule may stop earlier. Fine-tuning occurs afresh at each fitted iteration.

kNN uses five neighbours. Ranger uses 100 trees and XGBoost 30 boosting rounds. The seq10 variants use up to ten sequential passes; the other ranger/XGBoost variants predict each target from the same incomplete table. TabICL’s pretrained budget differs from these fitted models, so this is a practical method comparison.

Python >= 3.10 and the optional R package reticulate are required for TabICL. Install dependencies explicitly in the environment selected by reticulate:

python -m pip install -r inst/python/tabicl-requirements.txt
# From the repository root, with the current VIM installed and the Python
# environment selected via RETICULATE_PYTHON:
# Rscript vignettes/precompute.R tabiclImpute-benchmark
# Edit config in tabiclImpute-benchmark.Rmd.orig for a different experiment.
# Set VIM_TABICL2_RESULTS to a fresh local directory if configuration changes.
# To render the already cached document only:
rmarkdown::render("vignettes/tabiclImpute-benchmark.Rmd")

Datasets and preprocessing

  • Adult / Census Income, Becker and Kohavi (1996), DOI:10.24432/C5XW20: combine adult.data and adult.test (48,842 rows). Skip the test-file header, trim whitespace, remove the final period from test income labels, and parse ? as missing. Combining the published splits is intentional: this is transductive reconstruction of missing cells, not a supervised income test.
  • Bank Marketing, Moro, Rita and Cortez (2014), DOI:10.24432/C5K306: use bank-full.csv (45,211 rows), not the smaller sample or the different bank-additional-full.csv. Keep unknown as an observed category. It encodes recorded lack of knowledge; equating it with an artificially deleted value would change the evaluation target. Keep pdays = -1 (no prior contact) as a structural sentinel in its original numeric column. Do not interpret it as a literal negative duration.

Both UCI datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0. The script stores archive URLs and MD5 checksums for provenance. Raw records are downloaded only with explicit download = TRUE and are not bundled with VIM.

All character columns become unordered factors and all numeric measurements remain numeric. No clipping, logarithms, balancing, rare-level pooling or one-hot conversion is applied in shared preprocessing. Adult’s fnlwgt remains a predictor, not a survey weight; these are unweighted sample diagnostics. Both education representations are retained. Bank’s call duration is retained: it is available for retrospective imputation, but would be inappropriate in a pre-call subscription prediction task.

Remove rows with any existing NA to obtain complete references. Consequently, Adult results describe its complete-case population and need not transfer to people with naturally missing occupation or workclass. No correctness claim is made for the unobserved true values in those removed rows.

Missingness simulation

Each repetition draws a new simple random sample without replacement from each complete-case dataset at ** 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000 rows, with 3 repetition(s)** per scenario. The seed schedule is shared across sizes, so samples overlap and sample-size comparisons are not independent replications. The sampling algorithm may change with the requested size; exact nesting is not assumed. All methods share the same sample and mask within each dataset/size/repetition/mechanism/rate scenario. The column n records the number of rows in every result table. Seeds and training budgets are unchanged across sizes: more rows imply more observed context and, when fine-tuning is enabled, more training batches. The targets are Adult hours_per_week and income, and Bank balance and y. Other columns stay observed, including the MAR driver age.

makeMissing() selects exactly round(rate * nrow(truth)) cells per target, without replacement. MCAR uses uniform sampling. MAR uses weights = c(age = 1) explicitly: the sampling weights are the logistic transform of standardized observed age. These weights are not marginal cell-deletion probabilities; the requested number of rows is sampled using those relative weights. Higher age favours selection. Age is never masked, and no target’s hidden value drives another target’s missingness. Using the default MAR drivers instead could include the other incomplete numeric target, so specifying the observed driver matters here.

The where attribute supplies the common mask for every competing method and for scoring. We retain the original reference separately. With 250 rows, the three requested rates correspond to 25, 50 and 100 masked cells in each target. With other sample sizes the fractions may differ slightly due to rounding. Masks are never redrawn to remove difficult cases.

prepared <- uci_prepare("uci-cache", download = FALSE)
set.seed(config$seed)
truth <- prepared$data$Adult[sample(nrow(prepared$data$Adult), config$n[1L]), ]
incomplete <- makeMissing(truth, prop = .2, mechanism = "MAR",
  vars = c("hours_per_week", "income"), weights = c(age = 1), seed = config$seed)
mask <- attr(incomplete, "where")
incomplete <- droplevels(incomplete) # no levels learned solely from masked values
# truth is passed only to evaluation, never to a learner.

Evaluation

The pointwise metrics reuse VIM’s existing tools and score artificially masked cells only:

  • evaluation() supplies numeric mean squared error (err_num) and the fraction of incorrect categories (err_cat). We report RMSE as sqrt(err_num), misclassification as err_cat, and accuracy as 1 - err_cat. Because the current implementation of evaluation() sums errors over the supplied table, the runner subsets its inputs to masked cells for each target and passes an all-TRUE where matrix. This makes the scoring boundary explicit. Whole-table calls are equivalent only when observed values are preserved, which the runner also checks.
  • nrmse(x, y, m = mask) supplies NRMSE, using the standard deviation of the masked true values, as implemented by VIM. This is the convention used by the companion benchmark. Fewer than two masked values or zero masked-reference variance gives an undefined score, recorded as NA.
  • NRMSE_ref (nrmse_reference in the CSV) retains the alternative RMSE / sd(full sampled reference column) requested for this UCI benchmark. It is separate from VIM’s masked-reference NRMSE; under MAR the two denominators can differ substantially. Both denominators are common across methods within a scenario and are used only for evaluation.
  • MAE, whole-table marginal distances and relationship diagnostics supplement these existing tools; they are not available from evaluation() itself.

The following tables retain number of rows, dataset, mechanism and nominal rate. Scores are means across successful repetitions, with their sample standard deviations in parentheses. Counts are shown so failures cannot improve a ranking invisibly. The saved configuration has 3 repetition(s). With one repetition, standard deviations are unavailable; with few repetitions they describe variation only roughly. They are not confidence intervals or significance tests. Methods are paired by sample and mask, so formal comparisons would require paired analysis and more repetitions. Empty cells or NA indicate unavailable metrics: numeric error measures do not apply to categorical targets, classification accuracy does not apply to numeric targets, and a standard deviation requires at least two successful repetitions. These are missing summary statistics, not unfilled imputation cells. Auxiliary hurdle-model *_zero_prob diagnostics are excluded from the scored data; actual target columns must contain no missing values. Success counts use completed attempts as the denominator. The Coverage column distinguishes pending requested repetitions from scenarios outside the saved experiment.

Limitations and provenance

The configured repetitions provide descriptive comparisons. Scores apply to the complete-case populations and artificial target missingness; they do not assess proper multiple-imputation coverage. Pretraining overlap with these datasets has not been independently audited. Runtime includes model initialization, fitting, prediction and scoring, so checkpoint caching and hardware affect comparisons. The runner records failures and warnings, package/Python versions, sample indices, truth, masks and completions. Observed values and table schema are checked before scoring. Raw UCI records and weights are not bundled with this vignette.
